avoid anything that could be stressful
try hard not think about the trauma

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

Negative Appraisals.value: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me
I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
I have permanently changed for the worse

issues.item: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies are strongly social-evaluative and interpersonal (avoiding evaluation, avoiding conflict, rehearsing conversations), which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type of natural disaster and with the rest of the profile, which contains no social threat, shame, or interpersonal trauma content to explain these strategies.

issues.item: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
issues.explanation: Within the cognitive formulation, the strongest pathway is Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies. However, the selected negative appraisals focus on global identity change, chronic misery, and self-blame for being in the situation, while the selected strategies are specifically about managing social scrutiny and interpersonal interactions. That is a weak clinical fit: the strategies do not plausibly follow from the appraisals provided.

issues.item: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction
issues.explanation: Memory and appraisals are only partly coherent: terror on recall and olfactory recall fit disaster trauma, but rage on recall is less well supported by the rest of the profile because there is no accompanying appraisal about betrayal, preventability by others, or injustice that would explain intense anger as a central recall response.

For a natural-disaster trauma, intense rage specifically on recall is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which otherwise centers on terror, misery, self-change, and generalized avoidance rather than anger at a person or agent. Rage can occur, but here it lacks support from the other selected items and is the least coherent memory item.

'Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation' implies preventable personal failure in getting into the trauma. With a natural disaster, this appraisal is difficult to justify unless there was a very specific risky decision context, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile. The other appraisals focus on post-trauma change and unhappiness, making this item the clearest mismatch.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, strong self-blame framed as 'the event happened because of the way I acted' is hard to justify clinically unless the disaster involved a very specific preventable action by the patient. In the absence of any such context, this appraisal is implausible for the indexed trauma.

issues.item: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies are predominantly interpersonal/social-safety behaviors (avoiding conflict, rehearsing conversations) that fit social threat or shame-based trauma formulations more than a natural disaster PTSD presentation. They do not connect well to the memory/appraisal content provided.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: The profile includes active hypervigilant threat-monitoring ('constantly scan environment for signs of threat') and a global danger appraisal, but the formulation specifies Threat as effectively inactive, with no active links involving Threat and no active Trigger pathways. For a natural-disaster case, these items imply an ongoing threat-focused maintenance pattern that is not supported by the stated formulation.

issues.item: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place
issues.explanation: This is not just a weak-edge issue: both items explicitly center current external danger/threat, whereas the active formulation is concentrated on Negative Appraisals ↔ Memory and Negative Appraisals ↔ Maladaptive Strategies without Threat involvement. The remaining items fit a self-focused/post-traumatic change formulation, making these threat-focused items the main incoherent elements.

vignette:
Ethan sits stiffly in the chair, his hands clenched in his lap. At nineteen, he carries himself with the caution of someone much older. It has been eight months since the storm and the flash flood that followed, eight months since he found himself trapped in the basement of his family home as murky, brown water surged through the window wells. He can still see it, not as a continuous film but in a series of terrifying snapshots: the water swirling around the legs of the old couch, his high school yearbooks floating and then sinking, the water line climbing relentlessly up the concrete wall. These visual memories are the most persistent, appearing without warning and bringing with them the original, heart-stopping terror of drowning in the dark. Each time an image flashes into his mind, it serves as visceral proof for the belief that has taken root in his mind: he is permanently changed for the worse. The experience has left an indelible mark, and the happy, easygoing person he was before the flood is gone, replaced by this anxious stranger he no longer recognizes.

This profound conviction that he is irrevocably damaged now seems to govern his memory. Because Ethan believes he is broken, his mind seems to constantly scan for evidence, and in doing so, it frequently dredges up the very memories he is trying to escape. When he lies awake at night, convinced he will never feel true happiness again, his mind involuntarily returns to the basement. He'll suddenly catch the phantom smell of damp earth and sewage, a sensory echo that makes the memory feel terrifyingly present. He has come to believe that these intrusive recollections are not just symptoms, but a confirmation of his damaged state, his brain replaying the trauma as if to remind him of the exact moment he was ruined. This constant mental replay leaves him exhausted and steeped in a misery he cannot shake, reinforcing his sense of a lost, happier self.

Based on this deeply held belief that he is fragile and permanently altered, Ethan has constructed a life of careful, rigid avoidance. He is certain that he cannot handle any additional stress, that any strong emotion might shatter his already precarious composure. This fear has led him to systematically withdraw from his life, avoiding parties with friends, loud music, and even action movies-anything he thinks could be overwhelming. At his job at a fast-food restaurant, the simple act of social interaction has become a source of dread. Convinced he is no longer the same person, he feels deeply insecure, and so he meticulously rehearses what he needs to say before every single interaction, from greeting a customer to asking a manager a question. This constant preparation is a shield against the perceived stress of a spontaneous conversation, which he feels he is no longer capable of navigating.

These very strategies, however, only serve to tighten the loop of his distress. The immense effort he expends trying to suppress thoughts of the flood is a constant, draining battle; when the images inevitably break through, he sees it not as a normal trauma response, but as a personal failure, further evidence of his permanent damage. At work, after successfully navigating an interaction by relying on his script, he feels no relief, only a profound sense of alienation from himself. The need to rehearse a simple "Welcome, can I take your order?" confirms his most painful belief: the person he has become is unrecognisable to him. This exhausting cycle of effort and self-recrimination has left him feeling more isolated and miserable than ever. He finally sought help after an incident last week, when a coworker dropped a mop bucket, and the splash of grey water sent him into a full-blown panic attack in the breakroom. He is here now, quietly terrified that his worst fear is true, but holding onto a desperate hope that he might one day feel like himself again.
